question: Four mental shortcuts, four everyday traps. Which bias catches you in which moment?
answer: The one people miss is anchoring. A crossed-out price looks like information about value; it is there to set the ruler. In one experiment a rigged wheel stopping on 10 or 65 moved people's guesses of Africa's share of UN members from 25% to 45%.
move: A bias you can name in the moment is one you can step around.

pairs.right: The 'was $400' tag that makes $199 feel cheap
pairs.note: The first number you see becomes the ruler for every one after it.

pairs.right: Sitting through a bad film because you paid
pairs.note: The money is gone either way. Only the next two hours are still yours.

pairs.right: Fearing the flight more than the drive there
pairs.note: Crashes make the news. Car deaths are too common to.

pairs.right: 'The kitchen will take two weeks, tops'
pairs.note: We plan the best case and forget the delays every past job had.

source: Tversky and Kahneman, Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases, Science 1974

question: Four true findings that point the wrong way. Which trap is hiding inside each one?
answer: The schools are the one people miss. Small schools top the rankings and also fill the bottom: with few pupils, a handful of bright or struggling ones swings the average. The Gates Foundation spent about $1.7 billion splitting up big schools before anyone checked the bottom of the list.
move: Before trusting a pattern, ask who is missing and how many were counted.

pairs.right: Planes come home shot in the wings. Armour them?
pairs.note: Planes hit in the engines never came home. Armour where the holes aren't.

pairs.right: The top-scoring schools are mostly small ones
pairs.note: So are the worst. Few pupils, wild swings: small schools fill both ends.

pairs.right: Star rookies slump in their second season
pairs.note: A record year is part luck. The luck doesn't repeat; the talent does.

pairs.right: Countries with more storks have more babies
pairs.note: Bigger countries have more of both. Size drives each; storks don't.

source: Howard Wainer, The Most Dangerous Equation, American Scientist 2007; Robert Matthews, Storks Deliver Babies (p = 0.008), Teaching Statistics 2000

question: All of these cost you nothing to use. So who is really paying for each one?
answer: Pay in three is the one people miss. It feels like a loan, so you look for the interest, but the shop pays: a fee of a few per cent on every sale. Shops accept it because people spend more when the bill is split.
move: When something is free, find who pays, and what they get for it.

pairs.right: Market makers, paid to fill your orders
pairs.note: Payment for order flow. The SEC fined Robinhood $65M for hiding it.

pairs.right: A tiny few who spend a fortune
pairs.note: In one 2014 study, 0.15% of players brought in half the money.

pairs.right: Banks, when you take a card it suggests
pairs.note: The score is the bait. The fee comes when you sign up for the card.

pairs.right: The shop, giving up a cut of every sale
pairs.note: Shops pay a few per cent a sale, because people buy more in instalments.

source: SEC, press release 2020-321 on Robinhood; Swrve, Monetization Report 2014; Klarna Group, Annual Report 2024
